meta.title: Who really said "Hope is the thing with feathers - that perches in the soul"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it opens Emily Dickinson's poem J254/Fr314, written c.1861, first published 1891. Her original reads “Hope” in quotes, with a dash, not a hyphen.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hope is the thing with feathers - that perches in the soul'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Emily Dickinson: the opening of poem J254/Fr314 (c.1861), first printed 1891. Public domain. The popular form quietly drops her quotes around “Hope.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the genuine opening of Dickinson’s poem — catalogued J254 (Johnson) / Fr314 (Franklin) — copied into her hand-sewn Fascicle 13 around 1861 and first printed in Poems by Emily Dickinson, Second Series in 1891. Her own text reads “Hope” in quotation marks and joins the two lines with a dash, not a hyphen.

source.heading: The poem & its first printing

docMeta.dd: 1891, Poems by Emily Dickinson, Second Series (Roberts Brothers, Boston)

source.excerpt:
“Hope” is the thing with feathers —
That perches in the soul —
And sings the tune without the words —
And never stops — at all —
trail: The poem, its Johnson (J254) and Franklin (Fr314) numbers, its c. 1861 composition in Fascicle 13 and its 1891 first printing are documented at Wikipedia.
The full authenticated text is hosted by the Poetry Foundation and the Academy of American Poets.
The holograph manuscript survives in Fascicle 13 at Harvard’s Houghton Library.
source.excerptNote: Dickinson’s own wording keeps “Hope” inside quotation marks and uses her signature dashes; the widely shared “Hope is the thing with feathers - that perches in the soul” drops the quotes and flattens the dash to a hyphen.

source.rightsNote: Emily Dickinson died in 1886 and this poem was first published in 1891 — well before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — so the text is firmly in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Emily Dickinson
author.heading: About Emily Dickinson
author.bio: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) was an American poet who lived much of her life in near-seclusion in Amherst, Massachusetts, and published almost nothing while alive. After her death her sister found some 1,800 poems, many stitched into hand-sewn booklets called fascicles. Her compressed lines, slant rhyme and idiosyncratic dashes — on display in this poem — made her, posthumously, one of the central figures of American poetry.

misattribution.heading: It’s really hers — but the wording gets tidied up
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a famous quotation, the attribution here is correct: these are Dickinson’s own words. What travels online is a lightly altered rendering.

items.why: The popular form “Hope is the thing with feathers - that perches in the soul” drops the quotation marks Dickinson placed around “Hope” and replaces her line-ending dash with a hyphen; her text reads “Hope” is the thing with feathers — / That perches in the soul —, as shown at the Poetry Foundation.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are genuinely Dickinson’s — only her punctuation gets lost in transit, per the poem’s publication record.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Written around 1861, the poem casts hope as a small bird that “perches in the soul” and sings on regardless of the storm, never asking anything in return. Its plain ballad meter and gentle metaphor have made it one of the most quoted consolations in English.
